The president is poised to approve the start of negotiations between his leftist government and opposition leaders of five provinces who demand greater autonomy and the cancellation of a constitutional referendum that would give the president more power. The opposition also is angry over tax money that Morales is diverting from the provinces to fund elderly programs. Morales said the opposition leaders are trying to overthrow the government. "This is a coup in the past few days by the leaders of some provinces, with the takeover of some institutions, the sacking and robbery of some government institutions and attempts to assault the national police and the armed forces," Morales said. Opposition leaders say they merely want their demands met. Police kept order Monday during a march by about 2,000 pro-government groups opposed to the violence in the provinces. The demonstrators marched past the U.S. Embassy in La Paz. Morales expelled the U.S. ambassador to Bolivia last week, blaming the American government for inciting the violence. The United States called the accusations "false and baseless" and said Bolivia was making a "grave mistake." Most of South America's leaders attended Monday's emergency summit, with the exception of President Alan Garcia of Peru. Protest leaders asked to attend the summit in Santiago, Chile, but it was limited to heads of state. The protests started 21 days ago in Pando, Beni, Santa Cruz, Tarija and Chuquisaca provinces. The opposition groups have blockaded major roads and threaten to disrupt the nation's natural gas shipments, particularly to Brazil and Argentina. Anti-government protesters also have clashed with police and taken over offices and buildings in the five provinces.  Watch some of the violent demonstrations across Bolivia » . Much of the violence has taken place in Pando -- Morales declared martial law there Friday. On Monday, supporters of Morales, or his so-called militias, were gathering in Santa Cruz, and threatening to encircle the city, stoking fears that blood could be shed there. In Pando, it was reported that arbitrary arrests were taking place as the military took to the streets. Houses had been broken into and shot up, and civic leaders were fleeing to Brazil. It was uncertain, meanwhile, whether the Bolivian military remained solely behind Morales. Some signs of divisions had been seen within the military. Opposition leaders say they will not negotiate if there are any more deaths. Vice President Alvaro Garcia said the government will not negotiate about the dead citizens but will rigorously pursue those responsible for the killings. There are conflicting reports over who killed the 30 peasants. Opposition leaders say the peasants were ambushed by local forces. The government says the peasants were armed and initiated the firefight. The opposition has offered to lift the blockades as a goodwill gesture, but the government demanded that the protesters also relinquish the buildings and other property they have seized. Morales, Bolivia's first indigenous president, was elected in December 2005. CNN's Ione Molinares and Journalist Martin Arostegui contributed to this report.

LA PAZ, Bolivia (CNN) — Leaders of South American nations expressed support Monday night for Bolivian President Evo Morales, who has accused opposition leaders of attempting to overthrow his government.

Indigenous people from El Alto, Bolivia, took part in an anti-U.S. demonstration in La Paz on Monday.

Facing their first major crisis, members of the four-month-old Union of South American Countries voted to establish a commission to support Morales’ democratically elected government, Chilean President Michelle Bachelet said. Bachelet read a nine-point statement on Chilean television calling for the defense of human rights and democracy, as well as the preservation of Bolivia’s territorial integrity.

The statement condemned any attempts to overthrow the government. It also said the new commission would investigate a reported massacre in the Bolivian state of Pando, where violent clashes killed 30 people last week. Those clashes involved supporters of eastern governors seeking autonomy and backers of the central government.

South American leaders also urged dialogue to resolve Bolivia’s internal disputes.

Morales attended the emergency meeting of the union, which is modeled on the European Union and aims to promote political and economic integration among South American countries.

The president is poised to approve the start of negotiations between his leftist government and opposition leaders from five provinces, who are demanding greater autonomy and the cancellation of a constitutional referendum that would grant the president expanded powers. The opposition also objects to tax revenue that Morales is redirecting from the provinces to fund programs for the elderly.

Morales has said opposition leaders are attempting to overthrow the government.

“This is a coup in the past few days by the leaders of some provinces, with the takeover of some institutions, the sacking and robbery of some government institutions and attempts to assault the national police and the armed forces,” Morales said.

Opposition leaders say they are seeking only to have their demands met.

Police maintained order Monday during a march by about 2,000 pro-government demonstrators opposing the violence in the provinces. The demonstrators marched past the U.S. Embassy in La Paz.

Morales expelled the U.S. ambassador to Bolivia last week, accusing the American government of inciting the violence. The United States called the accusations “false and baseless” and said Bolivia was making a “grave mistake.”

Most South American leaders attended Monday’s emergency summit, with the exception of Peruvian President Alan Garcia. Protest leaders asked to attend the summit in Santiago, Chile, but participation was limited to heads of state.

The protests began 21 days ago in the provinces of Pando, Beni, Santa Cruz, Tarija and Chuquisaca. Opposition groups have blockaded major roads and threatened to disrupt Bolivia’s natural gas shipments, particularly to Brazil and Argentina.

Anti-government protesters have also clashed with police and seized offices and buildings in the five provinces.

Much of the violence has occurred in Pando, where Morales declared martial law on Friday.

On Monday, supporters of Morales, or his so-called militias, were gathering in Santa Cruz and threatening to encircle the city, heightening fears of further bloodshed.

In Pando, reports indicated that arbitrary arrests were taking place as the military moved into the streets. Houses had been broken into and shot up, and civic leaders were fleeing to Brazil.

Meanwhile, it remained uncertain whether the Bolivian military stood fully behind Morales. Some signs of division within the armed forces had emerged.

Opposition leaders say they will not negotiate if there are any more deaths.

Vice President Alvaro Garcia said the government would not negotiate over the deaths of citizens but would vigorously pursue those responsible for the killings.

There are conflicting accounts of who killed the 30 peasants. Opposition leaders say the peasants were ambushed by local forces. The government says the peasants were armed and initiated the firefight.

The opposition has offered to lift the blockades as a goodwill gesture, but the government has demanded that protesters also relinquish the buildings and other property they have seized.

Morales, Bolivia’s first indigenous president, was elected in December 2005.

CNN’s Ione Molinares and journalist Martin Arostegui contributed to this report.

LA PAZ, Bolivia (CNN) — On Monday evening, South American heads of state expressed backing for Bolivian President Evo Morales, who has accused opposition figures of attempting to bring down his administration.

On Monday in La Paz, Indigenous residents from El Alto, Bolivia, joined an anti-U.S. protest.

Facing its first major test, the four-month-old Union of South American Countries agreed to form a commission in defense of Morales’ democratically chosen government, according to Chilean President Michelle Bachelet. Speaking on Chilean television, Bachelet presented a nine-point declaration that emphasized respect for human rights, democracy, and Bolivia’s territorial unity.

The declaration rejected any effort to topple the Bolivian government. It also stated that the newly created commission would look into an alleged massacre in Bolivia’s Pando state, where clashes the previous week left 30 people dead. The violence involved supporters of eastern provincial governors seeking greater autonomy and backers of the central government.

The regional leaders also called for negotiations as a way to resolve Bolivia’s internal conflicts.

Morales took part in the union’s emergency session. The organization, inspired by the European Union, seeks to deepen political and economic integration among South American nations.

The Bolivian president is expected to authorize the beginning of talks between his left-wing government and opposition leaders from five provinces. Those leaders are demanding increased autonomy and the cancellation of a constitutional referendum that would expand presidential authority. They are also angered by Morales’ decision to redirect tax revenue from the provinces to programs for older citizens.

Morales has charged that the opposition is trying to remove him from office.

“What has happened in recent days is a coup carried out by leaders of certain provinces, through the occupation of institutions, the looting and theft of some government offices, and attempts to attack the national police and the armed forces,” Morales said.

Opposition representatives insist they are only seeking fulfillment of their demands.

On Monday, police maintained order as roughly 2,000 pro-government demonstrators marched against the violence occurring in the provinces. The marchers passed the U.S. Embassy in La Paz.

The previous week, Morales expelled the U.S. ambassador to Bolivia, accusing Washington of encouraging the unrest. The United States rejected the allegations as “false and baseless” and said Bolivia was committing a “grave mistake.”

Most South American presidents attended Monday’s emergency summit, though Peruvian President Alan Garcia did not. Protest leaders requested permission to participate in the meeting in Santiago, Chile, but attendance was restricted to heads of state.

The unrest began 21 days earlier in the provinces of Pando, Beni, Santa Cruz, Tarija, and Chuquisaca. Opposition groups have blocked key highways and have threatened to interfere with Bolivia’s natural gas exports, especially to Brazil and Argentina.

Anti-government demonstrators have also fought with police and seized government offices and other buildings across the five provinces.

Much of the bloodshed has occurred in Pando, where Morales imposed martial law on Friday.

On Monday, Morales supporters — described by some as militias — were assembling in Santa Cruz and warning that they might surround the city, heightening concerns that more violence could occur there.

In Pando, reports said arbitrary arrests were happening as soldiers moved through the streets. Homes had reportedly been entered by force and fired upon, while civic leaders were escaping to Brazil.

At the same time, it remained unclear whether Bolivia’s military was fully united behind Morales. There had been some indications of divisions within the armed forces.

Opposition leaders have said they will refuse to negotiate if any additional deaths occur. Vice President Alvaro Garcia said the government would not bargain over the dead but would aggressively pursue those responsible for the killings.

Accounts differ over who killed the 30 peasants. Opposition leaders say local forces ambushed them, while the government says the peasants were armed and began the shooting.

The opposition has proposed ending the roadblocks as a gesture of goodwill, but the government has insisted that protesters must also give up the buildings and other property they have occupied.

Morales, Bolivia’s first Indigenous president, was elected in December 2005.

CNN’s Ione Molinares and journalist Martin Arostegui contributed to this report.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about South American leaders backing Evo Morales during Bolivia’s 2008 political crisis, including the UNASUR summit, opposition autonomy demands, violence in Pando, and tensions with the United States.
counterfactuals.output:
**South American leaders rally behind Evo Morales amid Bolivia crisis**

*Santiago, Chile* — South American leaders threw their support behind Bolivian President Evo Morales on Monday during an emergency summit aimed at defusing a deepening political crisis marked by violent clashes, regional autonomy demands and rising tensions with the United States.

Meeting in the Chilean capital under the banner of the Union of South American Nations, or UNASUR, presidents from across the region issued a strong statement backing Bolivia’s democratically elected government and rejecting any attempt to destabilize it.

The summit came after weeks of unrest in Bolivia’s eastern lowlands, where opposition governors and civic leaders have demanded greater autonomy from Morales’ central government. The opposition-controlled departments — including Santa Cruz, Beni, Pando and Tarija — have pushed for more control over land, local governance and revenues from Bolivia’s natural gas reserves.

Morales, Bolivia’s first Indigenous president, has accused his opponents of trying to divide the country and undermine his reform agenda, which includes nationalizing key industries and rewriting the constitution to expand Indigenous rights.

The crisis escalated sharply after deadly violence in the northern department of Pando, where clashes between government supporters and opposition groups left numerous people dead. Bolivian authorities described the killings as a massacre of pro-Morales peasants and declared a state of siege in the region. Pando’s opposition governor, Leopoldo Fernández, was later detained by government forces, accused of involvement in the violence.

At the UNASUR summit, regional leaders condemned the bloodshed and called for dialogue, while making clear that they recognized Morales as Bolivia’s legitimate president.

“The countries of South America will not accept any break in the constitutional order,” the leaders said in a joint declaration, according to regional reports. The statement also called for an investigation into the Pando violence and urged all sides in Bolivia to seek a peaceful political settlement.

Chilean President Michelle Bachelet, who hosted the meeting, said the gathering reflected the region’s commitment to resolving South American conflicts without outside intervention. Leaders from countries including Argentina, Brazil, Venezuela, Ecuador and Colombia attended or sent high-level representatives.

The summit was also a sign of UNASUR’s emerging role as a regional diplomatic body. Formed earlier in 2008, the bloc sought to provide South American governments with a forum to address crises independently of Washington or the Organization of American States.

Tensions between Bolivia and the United States formed a major backdrop to the crisis. Morales had recently expelled U.S. Ambassador Philip Goldberg, accusing him of conspiring with opposition leaders — an allegation Washington denied. The United States responded by expelling Bolivia’s ambassador.

Morales’ allies, including Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez, accused the United States of supporting efforts to weaken leftist governments in the region. U.S. officials rejected the claims and said Bolivia’s internal problems should be resolved through democratic dialogue.

The confrontation highlighted the broader ideological divide in Latin America at the time, with Morales aligned closely with Chávez and other left-leaning leaders who criticized U.S. influence in the region.

Despite the show of support in Santiago, Bolivia remained deeply polarized. Opposition leaders insisted their autonomy movement was democratic and reflected legitimate demands from the country’s wealthier eastern provinces. Morales’ supporters said the movement was driven by elites resisting social and economic reforms.

The UNASUR declaration gave Morales an important diplomatic victory, reinforcing regional recognition of his government at a moment of acute pressure. But leaders also urged him and the opposition to enter negotiations, warning that continued confrontation could further destabilize the country.

For Bolivia, the challenge remained whether political dialogue could bridge a divide shaped by ethnicity, class, regional power and control over natural resources — or whether the violence in Pando would mark the beginning of an even more dangerous phase in the country’s crisis.

counterfactuals.output:
**BREAKING NEWS — LA PAZ, Bolivia**

Bolivian President Evo Morales has accused opposition-led regional governments of mounting what he called a “civil coup” against his administration, as anti-government protests, road blockades and violent clashes deepened the country’s worst political crisis in years.

Speaking in La Paz, Morales charged that conservative governors in Bolivia’s eastern lowland departments were seeking to destabilize his government after failing to defeat him at the ballot box. He said the unrest — centered in the resource-rich regions known as the “Media Luna,” including Santa Cruz, Beni, Pando and Tarija — was part of an orchestrated effort to divide the country and undermine democratic institutions.

“This is not a simple protest,” Morales said. “This is a coup attempt by groups that do not accept the will of the people.”

The accusations came after days of escalating confrontation between government supporters and opposition groups demanding greater autonomy and control over regional revenues, particularly income from natural gas fields. Demonstrators in opposition strongholds have seized public buildings, blocked highways and disrupted fuel supplies, while pro-government peasant and Indigenous organizations have mobilized in defense of the Morales administration.

### Regional protests and blockades

The crisis has been most intense in Bolivia’s eastern and southern departments, where opposition governors have rejected key elements of Morales’s political agenda, including a new constitution aimed at expanding Indigenous rights, increasing state control over natural resources and redistributing land.

In Santa Cruz, Bolivia’s economic hub and a center of anti-Morales activism, protesters have staged mass demonstrations and occupied government offices. Roadblocks have cut off transport routes, slowing food and fuel deliveries and raising fears of shortages. Similar protests have been reported in Tarija, home to some of Bolivia’s most important natural gas reserves, as well as in Beni and Pando.

Opposition leaders deny they are attempting a coup. They say Morales is using the charge to criminalize regional demands for autonomy and to distract from what they describe as an increasingly centralized and confrontational government. They argue that eastern departments generate much of Bolivia’s wealth and should have greater authority over local budgets, land policy and resource management.

But the Morales government says the protests have gone beyond legitimate dissent. Officials accuse opposition activists of attacking state institutions, sabotaging pipelines, intimidating government workers and inciting violence against Indigenous and peasant supporters of the president.

### Pando killings heighten tensions

The most serious violence occurred in the northern department of Pando, where deadly clashes between pro-government peasants and armed opposition supporters left multiple people dead. Government officials described the incident as a massacre of Morales supporters, saying peasants were ambushed while traveling to a political gathering.

The killings in Pando have become a flashpoint in the crisis. Morales’s government blamed local opposition authorities and moved to assert control in the department, declaring emergency measures and sending security forces to restore order. Authorities also pursued legal action against regional officials accused of involvement in the violence.

Opposition figures have disputed the government’s account, saying the situation was chaotic and that both sides were armed or mobilized. Human rights groups and church leaders have called for an independent investigation, warning that the country is moving dangerously close to wider internal conflict.

In La Paz, pro-government demonstrators gathered outside the presidential palace, chanting support for Morales and accusing the opposition governors of seeking to split Bolivia along racial, regional and class lines. Many Morales supporters say the conflict reflects resistance by old political and landowning elites to Bolivia’s first Indigenous president.

### Morales seeks regional backing

As the crisis intensified, South American leaders rallied behind Morales, expressing support for Bolivia’s elected government and warning against any attempt to remove him by force.

Presidents from across the region convened emergency consultations under the banner of South American diplomacy, with leaders including Brazil’s Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Argentina’s Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, Venezuela’s Hugo Chávez, Ecuador’s Rafael Correa and others voicing concern over the violence and backing Bolivia’s constitutional order.

Regional governments called for dialogue between Morales and the opposition governors while rejecting separatism and political destabilization. Several leaders said that any challenge to Morales must occur through democratic means, not through violence or the occupation of state institutions.

The international support was a political boost for Morales, who has framed the confrontation as a test of democracy in Bolivia and of regional solidarity against anti-government destabilization.

### Deep divide over autonomy and constitution

At the heart of the conflict is a long-running struggle over Bolivia’s political future. Morales, elected with strong support from Indigenous and working-class voters, has pursued a sweeping program of nationalization, land reform and constitutional change. His government says these reforms are necessary to reverse centuries of exclusion and inequality.

Opposition governors, backed by business groups and civic committees in the east, say Morales’s project threatens private property, regional economic autonomy and local democratic authority. They have pushed for departmental autonomy statutes, some approved in controversial regional votes that the central government considers illegal.

The dispute has sharpened Bolivia’s regional divide: the western highlands, where Morales remains highly popular, against the eastern lowlands, where opposition forces are strongest. It has also exposed ethnic and class tensions, with Indigenous peasant movements backing the government and urban middle-class and landowning sectors often aligning with the opposition.

### Calls for dialogue amid fears of escalation

Despite the harsh rhetoric, both domestic and international mediators are urging negotiations. Church officials, human rights advocates and neighboring governments have warned that continued blockades and confrontations could trigger further bloodshed and deepen the country’s economic crisis.

Morales has said he is willing to talk but insists that opposition leaders must first end the occupations, lift blockades and recognize the authority of the national government. Opposition governors say dialogue is impossible unless the government respects regional autonomy demands and stops using security forces and prosecutors against them.

For now, Bolivia remains on edge. Highways in several regions are blocked, government supporters are mobilizing, and security forces have been deployed to sensitive areas. The killings in Pando have hardened positions on both sides, making compromise more difficult.

Morales, however, has vowed not to back down.

“They want to overthrow an Indigenous president because we are changing Bolivia,” he told supporters in La Paz. “But the people will defend democracy.”

counterfactuals.output:
SANTIAGO, Chile (AP) — South American leaders rallied behind Bolivian President Evo Morales at an emergency summit Monday, pledging support for his democratically elected government as violent unrest and separatist tensions threatened to deepen a political crisis in Bolivia.

Meeting in Chile’s capital under the banner of the Union of South American Nations, or UNASUR, presidents and senior officials from across the region endorsed Bolivia’s constitutional order and rejected any attempt to break up the country or undermine Morales’ government.

The summit, convened by Chilean President Michelle Bachelet, came after clashes between Morales supporters and opponents in Bolivia’s eastern lowlands, where opposition governors have pushed for greater autonomy and resisted the president’s efforts to redistribute land and expand state control over natural resources.

In a joint declaration, the leaders expressed “full and firm support” for Morales and Bolivia’s institutions, condemned violence and called for dialogue between the government and opposition leaders. They also backed Bolivia’s territorial integrity, a key concern for Morales as autonomy movements gained strength in wealthier eastern provinces.

Morales, Bolivia’s first Indigenous president, has accused opposition leaders in the eastern departments of fomenting a coup and encouraging separatism. His opponents deny seeking to overthrow him, saying they are defending regional control over tax revenues and local governance.

The crisis intensified after deadly violence in the northern department of Pando, where government officials said peasants loyal to Morales were attacked by opposition-linked groups. Bolivian authorities declared a state of siege in the region and arrested the department’s governor, Leopoldo Fernández, whom they accused of involvement in the bloodshed.

UNASUR leaders agreed to support an investigation into the violence and urged both sides to halt confrontations. The regional bloc’s intervention marked one of its first major diplomatic tests since its creation as a forum for South American political coordination independent of Washington.

The meeting also highlighted a broad regional consensus against military or extra-constitutional solutions to political disputes. Leaders from countries with sharply different ideological orientations joined in backing Morales’ right to govern through his elected mandate.

Bolivia has been polarized for months between Morales’ leftist government, supported heavily by Indigenous and rural communities, and opposition-led eastern regions centered around Santa Cruz, where demands for autonomy have been tied to disputes over natural gas revenues, land reform and a new constitution.
